title: Simple cool-spot slopes have at most 20 percent recovery in a 30-day noise test of GJ 536 HARPS data
abstract: We test whether the published GJ 536 chromatic-index null can detect simple cool-spot wavelength slopes. A Planck contrast model has a 3685 K photosphere and seven spot temperature deficits from 200 to 1400 K. Its local missing-light velocity scale is set to 1.8 m/s at 550 nm. Two specified wavelength weight rules give slopes that we inject at 32.761 days into a conditional sign-block test of 195 public HARPS exposures. With 3999 draws, 30-day blocks and eight phases, recovery is 0.9 to 19.7 percent at a nominal 1 percent false-alarm threshold. The exact 500 minus 650 nm velocity scale is 0.031 to 0.373 m/s. Maximum recovery changes from 17.4 to 36.4 percent with 10- to 90-day blocks. A strong artificial slope gives about 92 to 97 percent recovery at 30 days. The chromatic null has low sensitivity to these model slopes. This does not show that spots cause the planet signal. The model does not explain its period or coherence and omits real line spectra, magnetic effects and surface geometry. No new independent observation or planet is found. Original code, aggregate evidence, a figure, source hashes and retrieval steps are supplied.

display.caption: Left: model wavelength response at a fixed 1.8 m/s scale at 550 nm. Right: conditional recovery over eight phases for two slope weight rules and 30-day noise blocks. These are model sensitivity results, not evidence for a spot origin.
